It gets handed to whoever is free, priced as an afterthought, and done with hand tools — which is exactly why so many Orlando homeowners end up with dust in the air handler and a slab their installer refuses to work over.

Manley Ohana does the opposite. Removal and interior demolition are the entire business. That means the ride-on scraper is already loaded, the vacuum shrouds are already on it, and the person operating it has twelve years on that specific machine instead of twelve jobs. It also means we have no reason to talk you into a floor — we are not selling one.

The deliverable is a clean slab: old covering gone, thinset and adhesive ground off, ridges taken down, debris hauled away and the floor swept. That is the condition your installer needs it in for their warranty to mean anything, and it is the condition we leave every job in — from a single Cocoa Beach condo to a whole house in Windermere.

How much does tile removal cost in Orlando?

It is priced by the square foot, and the number moves with what is under the tile and how it was set. Thinset on a concrete slab is the straightforward case; tile set over a wood subfloor, over a second layer of old tile, or with mortar beds runs higher because there is more to take off. Send a photo of the floor and the rough square footage and you will get a real number back, free and with no obligation.
How bad is the dust really?

Bad, if it is not controlled. Removing roughly 200 square feet of ceramic tile releases over a hundred pounds of silica dust, and on an untarped job that dust ends up in your HVAC returns, your closets and rooms nobody worked in — which is why the cleanup can outlast the demolition. We run shrouded, vacuum-fed equipment and seal off the areas we are not working in so the dust stays where the work is.
Do I need to move out while you work?

Usually not. Most of our jobs are done in occupied homes and occupied commercial buildings — we contain the work area, keep a clean path in and out, and take the floor out in stages where that makes sense. If a job genuinely needs the space empty for a day we will tell you that when we quote it, not after we have started.
Do you haul the debris away?
Yes. Removal, load-out and disposal are part of the job. You do not end up with a pile of broken tile in the driveway or a dumpster you have to arrange yourself, unless you would rather supply one.
Will the slab be ready for my new floor?

That is the point of hiring us. We grind off leftover thinset, mastic and adhesive and take down the ridges, then sweep the slab clean. Leaving that residue is what causes LVP and laminate to telegraph and what voids most installers' warranties — so if your installer finds something they cannot cover, we come back and correct it before they start.

Is old glue under vinyl a problem?

Concrete Floor Prep and Adhesive Grinding in Orlando, FL
Thinset, mastic and mortar ground off the slab with vacuum dust extraction, leaving a flat surface your installer will actually accept.

Getting the old covering off is only half the job. What is left behind — ridges of thinset, cutback adhesive, mortar-bed remnants, high spots — is what makes new vinyl plank telegraph, stops glue-down from bonding, and gives an installer grounds to walk away or void a warranty. We grind the slab back flat and clean with vacuum-shrouded equipment so the dust goes into a hose instead of into your air handler, then sweep it and hand it over ready to cover.
Why can't my installer just lay the new floor over the residue?

Some will, and it is the most common reason a new floor fails early. Adhesive residue stops glue-down products bonding, and any ridge or high spot under LVP or laminate shows through as a visible line and works the joints loose. Most manufacturers exclude that damage from warranty as an installation defect.
How do you keep grinding dust out of the house?

The grinder runs shrouded and connected to a vacuum, so the dust is captured at the head rather than released into the room. We also seal the openings to areas we are not working in. It is not a zero-dust process, but it is a fundamentally different one from open grinding.
Can you do prep only, if another company pulled the floor?

Yes. Prep-only calls are common — usually from a homeowner or an installer who has found the slab in worse condition than expected. Send a photo of what you are looking at and we will price the grind on its own.

Nailed, glued and floating wood floors pulled up clean, with the fasteners and adhesive taken off the subfloor behind them.

Nail-down hardwood leaves a field of fasteners that have to come out; glue-down engineered leaves adhesive that has to be ground off; floating laminate is fast but hides whatever the last installer left. We handle all three, take the residue with them, and leave the subfloor sound enough to cover again rather than a surface the next trade has to repair first.
Is hardwood removal less messy than tile?

Less silica dust, yes — but glue-down wood produces adhesive residue and nail-down produces a lot of splintered debris and hundreds of fasteners. We still contain the work area and still haul everything out, because a floor full of loose staples is not a floor anyone should be walking on.
Can you tell what is under my wood floor before starting?

Usually from a photo of an edge or a threshold, plus one lifted board if there is a spare closet. Knowing whether it is nailed, glued or floating is what makes the quote accurate, so it is worth the two minutes before we price it.
What if there is another floor underneath?

It is common in older Central Florida homes — wood over vinyl, or wood over the original tile. We will tell you what we find and price the second layer separately rather than discovering it mid-job and handing you a change order.

What Tile Removal Actually Does To The Air In Your House
Roughly 200 square feet of ceramic tile releases over a hundred pounds of silica dust. Here is where it goes on an uncontained job, and what containment actually looks like.

Most people booking a floor removal are thinking about noise and about how many days their house is unusable. Very few are thinking about the dust, and the dust is the part that outlasts the job.

## The number that surprises people

Breaking loose roughly 200 square feet of ceramic tile releases in excess of a hundred pounds of silica dust. That is a modest hallway and a bathroom — not a house. Scale it to the 1,200 square feet of tile that runs through the main living areas of a typical Central Florida home and the figure stops being an abstraction.

Silica dust is not ordinary house dust. The particles are fine enough to stay airborne for hours and small enough to be breathed deep into the lungs, which is why it is regulated as a workplace hazard rather than treated as a mess.

## Where it goes when nobody contains it

On an uncontained job, it does not stay in the room being worked.

It gets pulled into the return vents and distributed through the air handler to every room in the house, including the ones with the doors shut. It settles on top of kitchen cabinets, inside closets, on curtain rails, and in the tracks of every window. It works into upholstery. Homeowners describe finding it weeks later in rooms nobody set foot in — and dealing with it not as one clean-up but as several.

That is the actual cost people miss when they compare two removal quotes. The cheaper number frequently is cheaper because containment was never in it.

## What containment looks like in practice

There is no such thing as a genuinely dust-free demolition, and anyone promising one is selling something. There is a large and measurable difference between contained and uncontained, though, and it comes down to three things:

**Capture at the source.** The equipment runs shrouded, connected to a vacuum, so the dust is pulled into a hose at the point it is generated rather than released into the room and chased afterwards. This is the single biggest factor, and it is a function of what machine is on the trailer.

**Sealing what you are not working on.** Plastic over doorways and openings to areas outside the work zone. It is cheap, it takes twenty minutes, and it is skipped constantly.

**Protecting the HVAC.** If the return in the work area is left open, the system will happily distribute everything you just made. Covering it is not optional.

## What to ask whoever you hire

Ask whether the equipment is vacuum-shrouded or open. Ask whether containment and HVAC protection are included in the quoted price or billed separately. Ask what happens to the debris — whether haul-off is in the number or whether you will be arranging a dumpster.

If the answers are vague, the difference will show up in your house rather than on the invoice.

If the answers are vague, the difference will show up in your house rather than on the invoice.

Why Your Flooring Installer Rejected The Slab
The old floor is out, the room is empty, and the installer will not start. Almost always it comes down to leftover thinset, adhesive or a high spot — and to who was supposed to remove it.

It is one of the more common calls we take. Someone had their tile pulled up cheaply, the room is empty, the new flooring is stacked in the garage, and the installer has walked in, looked at the floor and said he cannot lay over that.

He is usually right.

## Removal and prep are two different jobs

Getting a covering off a slab and getting a slab ready to cover are not the same piece of work, and a lot of cheap removal quotes only include the first one.

When tile comes up, the thinset it was bedded in largely stays. When glue-down carpet or sheet vinyl comes up, a skin of mastic stays. What is left is a slab that is technically bare and functionally unusable — ridged, patchy, and in the case of adhesive, actively hostile to anything you try to bond to it.

## Why it matters more now than it used to

Twenty years ago most of what went back down was more tile, set in more thinset, which is forgiving about what is underneath it. Today most of what goes back down is luxury vinyl plank, and LVP is the opposite of forgiving.

It is thin and it is flexible, so it takes the shape of whatever is under it. A ridge of leftover thinset does not disappear beneath the plank — it shows through as a visible line across the floor, catches the light, and works the joints apart with every footstep until they separate. Manufacturers know this, which is why subfloor flatness and cleanliness are written into their installation requirements and why failures traced to them are excluded from warranty as installation defects rather than product defects.

So an installer refusing to start is not being difficult. He is declining to put his name on a floor that is going to fail and be blamed on him.

## What "ready to cover" actually means

- Old thinset, mortar and adhesive residue ground off, not just knocked down
- High spots taken flat
- No loose material, no fasteners, no tack strip left at the perimeter
- Swept clean, so the condition can actually be inspected

## If you are already in this position

Prep-only jobs are welcome and we take them regularly — usually from a homeowner whose removal contractor is not answering, or from an installer who arrived to a surprise. It is a grinding pass rather than a full removal, so it is priced accordingly.

Send a photo of the slab. It is generally clear from a picture whether you are looking at a light scuff pass or a full grind.
